```{r setup}
library(poscosea)
```

## Overview

In a binomial N-mixture model, counts \(y_{ij}\) are collected at sites
\(i = 1, \ldots, I\) on repeated visits \(j = 1, \ldots, J\):

\[
N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad
y_{ij} \mid N_i \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_i, p_{ij}).
\]

The data are hierarchical, so a bootstrap should resample both levels.
The **two-stage bootstrap** first resamples sites with replacement,
\(u \sim \mathrm{Mult}(I; 1/I, \ldots, 1/I)\), and then resamples the
observed visits within each selected copy of a site. Instead of refitting
the model for every resample, `poscosea` approximates each replicate of a
posterior mean from a single MCMC run:

\[
\theta^{(b)} \approx E[\theta]
  + \sum_{i}(u_{bi} - 1)\, c_i
  + \sum_{i,j}(v_{bij} - 1)\, e_{ij},
\]

where \(c_i\) and \(e_{ij}\) are posterior covariances between
\(\theta\) and the site-level marginal log-likelihood and the visit-level
log-likelihood, respectively.

The workflow is

1. `nmix_draws()` – pick \(\lambda\), \(p\) and \(N\) out of the MCMC output,
2. `nmix_loglik()` – compute the site- and visit-level log-likelihoods,
3. `ijk_nmix()` – compute the influence values for a quantity of interest,
4. `ijk_bootstrap_2stage()` – generate the bootstrap replicates.

## Example data

We simulate data with unmodelled overdispersion in abundance, so that the
fitted Poisson N-mixture model is misspecified.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
I <- 60; J <- 3
x  <- rnorm(I)                       # site covariate
xp <- matrix(rnorm(I * J), I, J)     # visit covariate
lambda_true <- exp(1.5 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(I, 0, 0.5))
N_true <- rpois(I, lambda_true)
y <- matrix(rbinom(I * J, rep(N_true, J), plogis(0.5 * xp)), I, J)
y[c(3, 10, 25), 3] <- NA             # some missing visits
```

## Posterior draws

In practice the parameter draws come from MCMC (see the last section).
To keep this vignette self-contained, we use a Laplace normal approximation
to the posterior of
\((\alpha_\lambda, \beta_\lambda, \alpha_p, \beta_p)\), with
independent weakly informative Normal priors specified below. These are
illustrative posterior draws, not MCMC output. The fitted Poisson model omits
the site-level abundance variation used to generate the data, so the resulting
intervals should not be read as calibrated coverage results. We draw
\(N_i\) from its conditional posterior. `nmix_loglik()` accepts a single
draw when evaluating the marginal likelihood during optimization.

```{r}
prior_mean <- c(1.5, 0, 0, 0)
prior_sd <- c(2, 1.5, 2, 2)

nll <- function(par) {
  lam <- matrix(exp(par[1] + par[2] * x), 1)
  p   <- matrix(plogis(par[3] + par[4] * xp), 1)
  log_lik <- sum(suppressWarnings(nmix_loglik(y, lam, p)$site))
  log_prior <- sum(dnorm(par, mean = prior_mean, sd = prior_sd, log = TRUE))
  val <- -log_lik - log_prior
  if (is.finite(val)) val else 1e10
}
opt <- optim(c(1, 0, 0, 0), nll, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
if (opt$convergence != 0) stop("Posterior mode optimization did not converge.")
post_cov <- solve(opt$hessian)

S  <- 2000
th <- t(opt$par + t(chol(post_cov)) %*% matrix(rnorm(4 * S), 4))
colnames(th) <- c("alpha.lam", "beta.lam", "alpha.p", "beta.p")

lambda <- exp(th[, 1] + outer(th[, 2], x))                   # S x I
p      <- plogis(th[, 3] + outer(th[, 4], as.vector(xp)))    # S x IJ

## N_i | y_i, theta on the grid max(y_i), ..., max(y_i) + 100
draw_N <- function(y, lambda, p, Nmax_extra = 100) {
  S <- nrow(lambda); I <- nrow(y)
  N <- matrix(NA_integer_, S, I)
  for (i in seq_len(I)) {
    obs <- which(!is.na(y[i, ]))
    Ns  <- max(y[i, obs]) + 0:Nmax_extra
    Nr  <- matrix(Ns, S, length(Ns), byrow = TRUE)
    lt  <- dpois(Nr, lambda[, i], log = TRUE)
    for (j in obs) lt <- lt + dbinom(y[i, j], Nr, p[, i + (j - 1) * I], log = TRUE)
    cw <- t(apply(exp(lt - apply(lt, 1, max)), 1, cumsum))
    N[, i] <- Ns[rowSums(cw < runif(S) * cw[, ncol(cw)]) + 1]
  }
  N
}
N <- draw_N(y, lambda, p)
```

## Log-likelihoods and influence values

`nmix_loglik()` returns the site-level marginal log-likelihood and two
versions of the visit-level log-likelihood: `obs_rb` (for quantities that
depend only on the parameters) and `obs_joint` (for quantities involving
the latent abundance \(N\); requires `N`).

```{r}
ll <- nmix_loglik(y, lambda, p, N = N)
str(ll[c("site", "obs_rb", "obs_joint")])
```

We draw the bootstrap weights once and share them across quantities.

```{r}
w <- nmix_weights(B = 5000, obs_mask = ll$obs_mask)
```

### A regression coefficient

```{r}
fit_beta <- ijk_nmix(th[, "beta.lam"], ll)
boot_two  <- ijk_bootstrap_2stage(fit_beta, type = "twostage", weights = w)
boot_site <- ijk_bootstrap_2stage(fit_beta, type = "site", weights = w)
boot_two
```

```{r}
rbind(
  posterior = c(estimate = mean(th[, "beta.lam"]), se = sd(th[, "beta.lam"]),
                setNames(quantile(th[, "beta.lam"], c(0.025, 0.975)), c("lower", "upper"))),
  site      = unlist(summary(boot_site)[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]),
  twostage  = unlist(summary(boot_two)[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")])
)
```

### The total abundance of the surveyed sites

\(\sum_i N_i\) depends on the latent abundance, so we use `obs = "joint"`.
The likelihood weights only capture the variation through the parameters;
`nmix_latent_resid()` adds the prediction error of \(N\).

```{r}
Ntot <- rowSums(N)
fit_N <- ijk_nmix(Ntot, ll, obs = "joint")
summary(ijk_bootstrap_2stage(fit_N, weights = w,
                             latent_resid = nmix_latent_resid(N, ll)))
quantile(Ntot, c(0.025, 0.975))      # posterior interval
sum(N_true)                          # realised value
```

### Several quantities at once: a regression curve

A matrix `theta` (draws in rows, quantities in columns) gives replicates for
all quantities with the same resamples.

```{r}
xg <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50)
lam_curve <- exp(th[, "alpha.lam"] + outer(th[, "beta.lam"], xg))   # S x 50
fit_curve <- ijk_nmix(lam_curve, ll)
sc <- summary(ijk_bootstrap_2stage(fit_curve, weights = w))
pq <- apply(lam_curve, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))

plot(xg, sc$estimate, type = "n", ylim = range(sc$lower, sc$upper, pq),
     xlab = "Site covariate", ylab = expression(lambda))
polygon(c(xg, rev(xg)), c(sc$lower, rev(sc$upper)), col = "grey80", border = NA)
polygon(c(xg, rev(xg)), c(pq[1, ], rev(pq[2, ])), col = "grey55", border = NA)
lines(xg, sc$estimate, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Two-stage bootstrap 95% CI", "Posterior 95% CrI"),
       fill = c("grey80", "grey55"), border = NA, bty = "n")
```

### Leave-one-site-out

The site-level influence values can be passed to `ijk_lko()`.

```{r}
loo <- ijk_lko(fit_beta$estimate, fit_beta$influence_site, k = 1)
plot(loo)
```

## Using MCMC output

With JAGS (here through `runjags`), monitor \(\lambda\), \(p\) and \(N\)
and pass the draws to `nmix_draws()`. Columns are matched by name
(`lam[i]`, `p[i,j]`, `N[i]`), so their order in the output does not matter.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(runjags)
fit <- run.jags("Nmix.txt", monitor = c("beta", "lam", "p", "N"),
                data = jags_data, n.chains = 3)
dr <- nmix_draws(as.mcmc.list(fit), I = nrow(y), J = ncol(y),
                 lambda = "lam", p = "p", N = "N")
ll <- nmix_loglik(y, dr$lambda, dr$p, N = dr$N)
```

If the detection model contains random effects, the monitored \(p_{ij}\)
are conditional on them and `nmix_loglik()` returns the likelihood
conditional on those random effects.
